display_title: Tensions Disrupt Shipping in Strait of Hormuz
display_title_he: מתיחות משבשת את הספנות במיצר הורמוז
short_summary: Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has plummeted to a two-month low due to a surge in attacks on oil tankers. Producers are now diverting exports to alternative routes to maintain global supply levels.

sources.title: צניחה חדה: שפל של חודשיים בתנועת המכליות במיצר הורמוז

paragraphs: The Strait of Hormuz, a critical artery for global energy supplies, is currently experiencing a significant and concerning decline in maritime traffic. According to data provided by the shipping analytics firm Kpler, the number of vessels traversing this strategic waterway reached its lowest point in over two months on October 8, 2026. On that specific day, only seven cargo ships were recorded passing through the strait, a figure not seen since July 23. While a modest recovery to ten vessels was observed the following Wednesday, the overall trend remains notably subdued compared to historical norms.

This downturn follows a sharp and dangerous escalation in regional hostilities. Security sources monitoring the area report that attacks on oil tankers have reached a weekly peak since the onset of the conflict with Iran. In a recent incident reported by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a tanker near Qatar was struck by projectiles, an event that unfortunately resulted in reported casualties. These persistent security threats have triggered a 27% drop in crude oil transit through the strait compared to the peak levels observed just one week prior. Current volumes, estimated at 10.1 million barrels per day, represent only 74% of the activity levels recorded before the conflict began, returning to the average seen throughout September.

Historically, the Strait of Hormuz served as a vital conduit for global trade. Before the outbreak of hostilities on February 28, approximately 125 large commercial vessels—including oil tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers, and container ships—passed through the strait daily. These shipments historically accounted for one-fifth of the world’s crude oil and liquefied natural gas supply. It is important to note that current data may not capture the full picture, as some vessels intentionally disable their automatic identification systems to avoid detection, meaning the actual volume of traffic could be higher than what is officially tracked.

Despite the volatility within the strait, Gulf oil producers have demonstrated remarkable resilience by pivoting to alternative export routes. Exports originating from the coasts of the Gulf of Oman and the Red Sea have surged to 6.7 million barrels per day, more than double the levels recorded before the conflict. This strategic shift has effectively compensated for the supply disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, particularly regarding ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, allowing the total volume of crude oil exports from the Middle East to remain consistent with pre-conflict levels. As the situation remains fluid, the industry continues to monitor the delicate balance between maritime security and the necessity of maintaining global energy flows.

facts.fact: Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz hit a two-month low on October 8, 2026, with only 7 cargo ships passing through.
Crude oil transit through the strait dropped by 27% compared to the previous week, reaching 10.1 million barrels per day.
Gulf oil producers have increased exports via alternative routes, such as the Gulf of Oman and the Red Sea, to 6.7 million barrels per day.
Attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz reached a weekly peak recently, including an incident near Qatar involving projectiles and casualties.
Before the conflict, approximately 125 large commercial vessels passed through the strait daily, accounting for one-fifth of global oil and LNG supply.
